article.title: New World Crimes
article.author: Peter Laarman
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Subjugation, domination, exploitation, extraction: it no longer strikes anyone as odd to associate these behaviors with Americans who are eager to call themselves Christians. But many observers also think of this excrescence as a new development in Christianity. If only!! Those with some grasp of the backstory can find a discernable line of descent from the English Puritans, a self-described “chosen” people who took it upon themselves to purify the Protestant project, ridding it of all popish residues. They began as dissenters in England only to end as theocrats here, crushing all dissent in governing their settlements in Connecticut and Massachusetts. They also took it upon themselves to dispossess, enslave, and murder Indigenous people here as part of “The Glorious Works of Christ in America” (the name given to the project by Puritan divine Increase Mather). This was happening while their Puritan counterpart back in the Mother Country—the Lord Protector, Oliver Cromwell—was colonizing Ireland in the name of safeguarding Protestantism from possible Catholic subversion. Twenty percent of Ireland’s population is believed to have died in this subjugation process. As I say, much of this is now well known. What fewer people pay attention to is what happened in late 15 th century Spain, before there was even such a thing as Protestantism. Not to give the killer Protestants a pass, but it would be hard to beat the Spain of Ferdinand and Isabella in respect to intolerance, cruelty, and ethnic cleansing dressed up as piety. Wanting to know more about Spain, I was glad to come across a tightly written and well-researched account of the convergence of reconquest, purification, and colonization by Their Most Holy Catholic Majesties, Ferdinand and Isabella. The book, by James Reston, Jr., is titled Dogs of God: Columbus, the Inquisition, and the Defeat of the Moors. “Dogs of God” was a label proudly worn by friars of the Dominican order, founded in the 13 th during the Church’s fraught effort to put down heretics in southern France. In Ferdinand and Isabella’s time, these tough Dominicans became central figures in the Spanish Inquisition, a campaign created to purge a united Spanish kingdom of all doctrinal impurity while consolidating royal power. The campaign was primarily focused on Christians suspected of having Jewish blood. The first Grand Inquisitor—the much-feared Torquemada , notorious for his brutal methods—was a Dominican. His agents “relaxed” (tortured) suspected heretics to get confessions, then burned them in spectacular displays called Acts of Faith . Licensed by the pope, the Inquisition’s reign of terror under Ferdinand and Isabella was complemented by these monarchs’ creation of a national police force to undermine the authority of regional nobles, widespread confiscations of nobles’ properties, imposition of a national currency, and unification by means of Castilian as a national language. All of this was suffused in lavish displays of piety. Isabella, a beautiful and brilliant leader, was especially deft at inviting comparisons of herself to the Virgin Mary, orchestrating gorgeous triumphal processions, and building shrines wherever she went. With a charismatic partner like this, a grim and tightlipped Ferdinand could focus on liquidating rivals and planning the military conquest of Moorish territory in the south. Fun fact: Niccolo Machiavelli modeled his cunning Prince on the calculating, ruthless Ferdinand. Related: Beyond Plantation Capitalism: Rev. Peter Laarman on the Fight for Economic Justice The First New World Conquistador: Columbus as Religious Zealot It is widely known that Columbus was an Italian sailor of humble origins who washed up in Spain looking for opportunity. He was also a mystic who was enthralled by the idea that he might not just find the riches of the East by sailing West: he might also somehow effectuate the reconquest of the Holy Land by Christians. Realizing how susceptible the pious Isabella was to this sort of jive, he eventually won her patronage by dangling Holy Jerusalem in front of her own crusading ambition. Reston vividly imagines the pitch made by a fame-hungry Genoese mariner to a receptive queen in 1489, on the eve of the final subjugation of the Moors in Granada and the subsequent expulsion of all unbaptized Jews from Catholic Spain: Discovery must join Reconquest and Purification. Together, the three fitted into the new heaven and the new earth that was promised in the Book of Revelation. Ferdinand, Torquemada, and Columbus were to be the queen’s—and God’s—instruments in a passion play. Columbus even promised the queen that if she would bankroll and bless his western adventure, he would contribute the profits to fund a glorious new crusade in the Holy Land. The monarchs weren’t ready to act just then, in 1489. They had other things on their mind. But in the flush of victory against Muslims in the south two years later—a central goal of Christian Europe for 800 years—and just as they were imposing their final solution upon a long-established Jewish population, the sovereigns finally gave Columbus the green light. Before casting off, he painted the sails of his little caravels with the Crusaders’ cross—the same square cross used by the Knights Templar. Enroute to his port of departure, Columbus encountered Jews fleeing for their lives: two nightmares unfolded at the very same moment. Related: Marlon James Uncovers Depths of Depravity in Evangelical Christianity Imperial Rivalry, Colonization, and Slavery By now, many people also know that New World colonization received the Church’s seal of approval by way of a papal bull (two bulls, actually) issued in 1493. This is the origin of the so-called Doctrine of Discovery . But there is more to know, and Reston supplies vital details. Ferdinand and Isabella were seriously haunted by the fear that rival Portugal might beat them to the punch in New World conquests. After all, Portuguese navigators were widely recognized to be the best in the world: they had sailed around the Cape of Good Hope, they had already established colonies in Africa, and they were on their way to colonizing India and capturing Asia’s lucrative spice market. Spain also knew their rival was aware that Columbus had found something very interesting on his first voyage: the admiral’s storm-wracked Nina had actually been forced to dock in Portugal before finally limping into Spanish waters. In view of this threat, Spain demanded that a Spanish pope (a splendidly debauched Alexander VI—Rodrigo Borgia by birth) grant them secure protection for the lands Columbus had “discovered.” So yes, Rome’s sanction for conquest was important, but ultimately more important was Spain’s direct negotiation with Portugal to divide up the globe. Intense negotiation led to a treaty in 1494, and in this treaty, Spain came up short. Portugal’s negotiators managed to re-draw the pope’s dividing line hundreds of miles to the west, with a major unanticipated bonus for Lisbon. In 1500, the Portuguese realized just what a sweet deal they had made when a fleet bound for India bumped into Brazil while taking an extreme western course in order to avoid navigation troubles closer to Africa. Not only could they keep all their rich possessions in Africa and India, but now they also had access to a vast lowland terrain ideal for growing sugar cane. As the Portuguese were already well into African slavery, and as they had already figured out how to grow and process cane sugar by way of their Eastern connections, they could and did put two and two together to start building a lucrative slavery-based sugar economy. Between 1501 and 1875, tiny Portugal would transport half of all the Africans delivered into New World bondage: some six million people in all. The Spaniards brutally enslaved people for the purpose of extracting precious metals; the Portuguese enslaved far more people in order to extract sugar from endless fields of cane. By the time the growing Dutch and British empires came along to horn in on Portugal’s sugar bonanza in the mid-17 th century, the New World’s sugar would be proving far more valuable than its silver and gold. Related: Curbing Cancerous Capitalism: An Organizing Challenge for the Ages White Christian Supremacy at the Dawn of Modernity All this backdrop may seem beside the point when thinking about today’s white Christian nationalism, but in fact it is highly relevant to understanding the incubation of a toxic strain. Although Ferdinand and Isabella initially rebuked Columbus for enslaving Indigenous Caribbeans (his second expedition was a wild festival of plunder), it was soon obvious to all Europeans that what they faced in the New World would be a labor shortage of staggering proportions, given the amount of land and resources available for exploitation. Enslaving the natives would never be sufficient; deploying indentured white labor wouldn’t cut it; African slavery emerged as the solution. The Christians even believed their anti-Black racism had a biblical warrant in the so-called “curse of Ham” in Genesis. In a word, churchly resistance to slavery quickly melted away. By the time an infant United States of America proclaimed its independence, the great majority of Christian preachers here were solidly convinced that chattel slavery was God’s will. And our “one drop rule” for racial purity? Why, that’s directly linked to the religious “purity of blood” ( limpieza de sangre ) demanded by Catholic Spain. As for territorial conquest, the North American Protestants may have hated everything else about the Church of Rome, but they were more than happy to adopt the Doctrine of Discovery for their own purposes. More to the point, it is impossible to separate our mostly Protestant version of white Christian nationalism from the Catholic version of 15 th century Spain. Why? Because Protestant rigidity and Protestant zealotry in England and Holland—the wellsprings of our current torments—were directly forged in reaction to the very real mortal threat posed by Catholic Spain, and later by Catholic France, to the entire Protestant project in Northern Europe. From the reign of Henry VIII all the way through the so-called Glorious Revolution of 1689, it was touch and go for the Protestant cause in Britain. The success of Dutch Protestant resistance to mighty Spain was viewed by the English as a minor miracle, but it hardly eased their fears; rather, it inspired greater vigilance and even the importation of a Dutch monarch. So there we have it: white Christian nationalism emerged side-by-side with what historians consider the birth of the modern era in 1492. We’ve suffered the consequences ever since.
